# The Tale of the First Shadow

Long ago, when the world was newly formed, there lived a young weaver named Selene who created the most beautiful tapestries under the blazing sun. The sun god, Helion, shone so brightly that no darkness existed anywhere in the world.

One day, Selene grew weary. "Great Helion," she called out, "your light is glorious, but I cannot rest. My eyes burn, and I long for respite."

Helion, in his pride, refused. "Darkness brings fear and uncertainty. My light protects all."

Desperate, Selene wove her finest tapestry yet—a cloth so thick and dark it could hold back even divine light. She held it above her head, and beneath it, the world's first shadow was born. In that cool darkness, she finally rested.

Helion was furious and reached down to tear the tapestry away. But when his fingers touched the shadow, he discovered something unexpected: beauty. The contrast made his light shine more brilliantly at the edges, creating stunning gradients of gold and amber.

Moved by this revelation, Helion agreed to rest each night, giving the world darkness. And so shadows were born—not as enemies of light, but as its eternal companions, making beauty possible through contrast.

Long ago, when the world was newly formed, a young goddess named Aria possessed the most beautiful voice in all creation. She would sing to the mountains, the rivers, and the sky, filling the silence with melodies that made flowers bloom and stars shine brighter.

But Aria was lonely. Though all of nature loved her songs, nothing could sing back to her. She wandered the earth, calling out, hoping for a reply that never came.

One day, heartbroken, she climbed to the highest peak and sang her saddest song—a melody of longing and solitude. As her final note faded, something miraculous happened. The mountains sang back to her, returning her own voice in a gentle, distant whisper.

Aria wept with joy. She sang again, and again the mountains replied. She had found her companion at last.

The other gods, moved by her discovery, blessed the world so that valleys, caves, and canyons would forever carry voices back to those who called out. This was their gift to Aria and to all who would ever feel alone.

And so, the echo was born—a reminder that even in our loneliest moments, the world listens and answers.

Stillwater replied softly, "And you destroy everything you touch. How can you bear leaving only ashes?"

Ember tempered her flames, heating the pond until steam rose in soothing clouds. The child bathed in the warm waters and survived the night.

The spirits finally understood: neither wildness nor stillness alone was complete. True wisdom lay in knowing when to burn bright and when to rest calm, when to act and when to receive.

They became partners, teaching that opposites need not conflict—they can create something neither could achieve alone.
